# Sirach Chapter 31 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Vaticanus, Sirach 31 | **Agents Consulted:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA

---

## Council Notes

Chapter 31 divides into two main sections: anxiety over wealth (vv. 1–11) and proper behavior at table with special attention to wine (vv. 12–31). The "evil eye" (v. 13) refers to covetousness or greed, not supernatural malice. Verse 27's praise of wine as "life" should be rendered with full weight — Ben Sira is not being ironic. The chapter contains one of antiquity's most balanced treatments of wealth: not condemned outright, but those who are rich and blameless deserve genuine honor.

---

**31:1** Sleeplessness over wealth wastes away the flesh, and anxiety about it drives away sleep.

**31:2** Anxious worry cuts off slumber, and a serious illness carries away sleep.

**31:3** The rich man toils in accumulating wealth, and when he rests he fills himself with pleasure.

**31:4** The poor man toils in poverty, and when he rests he becomes needy.

**31:5** Whoever loves gold will not be justified, and whoever pursues it will be led astray by it.

**31:6** Many have been brought to ruin because of gold, and their destruction came to meet them face to face.

**31:7** It is a stumbling block to those who sacrifice to it, and every fool will be ensnared by it.

**31:8** Blessed is the rich man who is found blameless, and who has not gone chasing after gold.

**31:9** Who is he? And we will call him blessed, for he has done wonderful things among his people.

**31:10** Who has been tested by it and found perfect? Let that be his glory. Who was able to transgress and did not transgress, and to do evil and did not do it?

**31:11** His prosperity will be established, and the congregation will declare his acts of charity.

**31:12** If you are seated at the table of a great man, do not open your gullet wide at it, and do not say, "How much there is on it!"

**31:13** Remember that the evil eye is a wicked thing. What has been created more evil than an eye? Therefore it weeps from every face.

**31:14** Do not stretch out your hand to everything your eye falls on, and do not crowd your neighbor in the serving dish.

**31:15** Judge your neighbor's feelings by your own experience, and be considerate in every matter.

**31:16** Eat what is set before you as a well-bred person would, and do not devour food greedily, lest you be despised.

**31:17** Be the first to stop eating out of good manners, and do not be gluttonous, lest you give offense.

**31:18** And if you are seated among many, do not reach out your hand before they do.

**31:19** How sufficient is a little for a disciplined man! He does not gasp for breath upon his bed.

**31:20** Sound sleep comes with moderate eating; he rises early and is at ease. But the pain of sleeplessness, nausea, and gripping colic attend the glutton.

**31:21** If you have been compelled to eat too much, get up, go out, and vomit, and you will find relief.

**31:22** Hear me, my child, and do not disregard me; in the end you will find my words true. In all your work be diligent, and no illness will overtake you.

**31:23** The generous man is spoken well of by everyone, and the testimony of his goodness is trustworthy.

**31:24** The miser has the city's complaint against him, and the testimony of his meanness is accurate.

**31:25** Do not show yourself valiant in wine-drinking, for wine has been the ruin of many.

**31:26** The furnace tests the tempered blade; so wine tests hearts in the quarrel of the proud.

**31:27** Wine is life for human beings when drunk in moderation. What life is there for a man without wine? For it was created to make people glad.

**31:28** Wine drunk at the proper time and in due measure is joy of heart and gladness of soul.

**31:29** Wine drunk to excess brings bitterness of soul, provocation, and stumbling.

**31:30** Drunkenness increases the rage of a fool to his own hurt, diminishing his strength and adding wounds.

**31:31** Do not rebuke your neighbor at a wine-feast, and do not humiliate him in his moment of celebration. Speak no word of reproach to him, and do not distress him by pressing demands.
